The observer effect doesn't work like that. Localized presence of matter collapses wave forms quite well in the absence of intelligent observation. There's only one solution to those quantum equations that doesn't phase one molecule into another.
Interesting. Can you elaborate or at least point me in the right direction? How can you tell if the wave form collapsed if there was no one around to record it? Sounds like a zen proverb.

It's an argument largely based on the Law of Large Numbers and simple logic, really. There does exist a wave function for every particle in an object large enough to be seen by the human eye, but even something as small as a coin is comprised of such a mind-bogglingly large number of molecules that the sum calculated waveforms of its exact quantum behavior are so close to the behaviors predicted by classic mechanics that there is no need to do all the work to get a good idea of what's going on. A large object's component forces (electromagnetic and gravity, mainly) also overrule any possible quantum deviations to the point where their effects also become zero on sufficiently large length scales. Furthermore, the proximity of nearby matter limits the list of valid quantum states the particle can occupy. While it is possible that a lone molecule may do strange things (like exist as a cloud of probability), as you increase the number of molecules and form bonds between them, there are fewer and fewer configurations possible for the system until any bizarre quantum probabilities go to zero. That's why coins and shirts don't seem to shuffle around like a waveform. The science is still out with respect to socks.
